attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated as his view.

semantics.note: The proposition is faithful. Because the second half says Meta's waste came from a mistaken hypothesis, it is causal, not a plain observation, as the contract's axis already recognises.

contract.note: The plain reading treats this as a compound claim: size alone does not determine performance, and Meta wasted spending because it relied on that idea. That is a fair, ordinary reading. 'Waste' and 'massive sums' have no stated measure.

evidence.note: A March 2025 preprint shows data filtering and training choices matter beyond size. It bears on the general point only, not on Meta's spending or what caused it.

Meta's own launch post (a company disclosure) describes MoE and other new pre-training approaches. This weakens a size-only account but does not establish Meta's internal expectations or whether money was wasted.

reviews.rationale: The general point that factors beyond size matter gets some backing from e1. The causal part is not established: no evidence shows Meta's project spending, its targets, a shortfall, or that it relied on size alone. e2 even suggests Meta tried more than scaling. The packet does not settle the compound claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'many' (not all) and the pundit-coverage scope that comes from the surrounding paragraph. It is an observation about the period before April 7, 2025.

contract.note: The plain reading (customers get little attention in the named pundits' coverage, and many customers are disappointed) is fair. 'Rarely' has no denominator, so the result depends on how coverage is defined.

evidence.note: WRITER's own survey release (a company disclosure; fieldwork ended Dec 2024, published before the post). Over a third of executives report major disappointment, which backs the 'many disappointed' part only. It says nothing about pundit coverage.
A May 2024 Hard Fork segment on listeners' AI use at work. One isolated example; it cannot show whether such coverage was rare or regular.
Newton's April 2024 criticism of the Humane pin, quoted secondhand. It shows attention to a disappointing product, not how often customers' own accounts appeared.

reviews.rationale: e3 backs the disappointment part for organisational adopters. Nothing in the packet counts or samples Roose, Newton and Cowen's coverage, so 'rarely mentioned' can be neither confirmed nor refuted. e4 and e5 are isolated examples. The main frequency claim is unsettled.

attribution.note: Marcus states this in his own voice; he does not attribute it to anyone else.

semantics.note: Dropping 'pretty' slightly strengthens the wording but does not change the commitment. It is an observation about the launch-period reaction.

contract.note: The plain reading (widespread, visible disappointment with performance, not unanimity) is ordinary and fair to the words. The April 5-7 window matches 'just-released'.

evidence.note: Ars Technica, April 7, 2025: a mixed-to-negative reception from the AI community, early performance tests disappointed experts, and Willison called the vibes 'decidedly mid'.
Lambert's firsthand disappointment, but he ties it partly to release strategy and access, not only to performance.

The same reviewer calls the evaluation scores solid. This is counterevidence on capability, but it sits alongside his note that LocalLlama was unhappy and that independent results ranged from medium to bad.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous reporting (e1) documents a visible mixed-to-negative reaction that centred on performance. Lambert adds that the LocalLlama community was unhappy and that independent results ranged from medium to bad. Some solid benchmark scores (e3) do not show a mainly favourable reaction. Under the plain reading, the claim is supported, though how widespread the disappointment was is not measured.

attribution.note: Marcus's own characterisation in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition rightly leaves out the hedged 'billion (?)' figure. The key term, 'what we might call GPT-5 level', is self-consciously loose and undefined.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to read in a later product called GPT-5 or an arbitrary benchmark threshold. Without a definition of the target, no fair criteria can be fixed.

reviews.rationale: 'GPT-5 level AI' has no operational or contemporaneous definition, and 'failed' depends on that undefined target. Any test would rest on a standard the speaker did not supply. The packet has no evidence items, and no fair measure exists, so the claim is too vague to score.
